questions.statement: A text begins: 'Read this notice carefully: all students must return library books on Friday.' What is the purpose of the text?
questions.context: A reading comprehension exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To tell readers what they are required to do
options.feedback: The notice gives an obligation, which is the purpose its form signals.

options.text: To describe how the library works
options.feedback: Only the return requirement is mentioned, not a description of the whole system.

options.text: To persuade students to enjoy reading more
options.feedback: No argument about reading habits appears in the notice at all.

options.text: To tell a story about a lost book
options.feedback: There is no narrative in the text; it is a set of instructions.

questions.explanation: The imperative verb 'must return' and the wording 'carefully' show that the writer wants readers to act on the information.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a text that lists the ingredients and steps for making a soup?
questions.context: A reading comprehension lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To argue that soup is better than other dishes
options.feedback: No comparison or opinion is offered in a recipe.

options.text: To explain how to prepare a dish
options.feedback: The sequence of steps gives instructions for cooking, which is the purpose.

options.text: To tell the history of the recipe
options.feedback: Nothing in the description concerns where the recipe came from.

options.text: To describe the taste of the soup
options.feedback: Taste would need adjectives about flavour, which the text does not include.

questions.explanation: A text that lists ingredients and steps is written so that a reader can carry out the process described.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the text and identify its purpose: 'Once you have read the chapter, answer the six questions at the end of page forty.'
questions.context: A reading comprehension exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To summarise the plot of the chapter
options.feedback: The text gives no plot information at all; it only directs the reader.

options.text: To persuade the reader to read further chapters
options.feedback: There is no argument encouraging the reader to continue.

options.text: To direct the reader to a task to carry out
options.feedback: The imperative 'answer' tells the reader what to do next, which is the purpose.

options.text: To provide background information about the author
options.feedback: Nothing in the instruction concerns the author.

questions.explanation: The instruction points the reader to a specific activity after reading, so the purpose is to direct the reader's next step.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A text describes how a new recycling system works in the city. What is its purpose?
questions.context: A reading comprehension lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To convince readers to oppose the system
options.feedback: An argumentative text would present reasons against it, which the text does not.

options.text: To narrate the life of a recycler
options.feedback: A narrative would tell a story with characters, which is absent here.

options.text: To entertain with a humorous account
options.feedback: Humour is not the register the description of the system uses.

options.text: To inform readers about how the system works
options.feedback: Explaining a process is an informative purpose, which matches the text.

questions.explanation: A text that explains how a system works is intended to inform the reader about the way it functions.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a text that reports the results of a scientific study?
questions.context: A reading comprehension task in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To sell a product to the public
options.feedback: Nothing in the description is commercial, and reports do not aim to sell.

options.text: To entertain readers with an unusual event
options.feedback: The purpose is factual rather than entertaining in a study report.

options.text: To teach a practical skill step by step
options.feedback: That would be an instructional text, not a report of findings.

options.text: To present findings and information about a study
options.feedback: A report of results exists to inform the reader about what was discovered.

questions.explanation: Reporting findings is an informative purpose: the writer's aim is to convey what the study discovered.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the text whose purpose is to entertain.
questions.context: A reading comprehension lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: A list of the dates of each school holiday
options.feedback: A list of dates is informative and serves no purpose to amuse.

options.text: A description of how to change a bicycle tyre
options.feedback: A set of instructions is instructional rather than entertaining.

options.text: A funny story about a student who lost his shoes on the way to school
options.feedback: The humour and the light plot aim to amuse the reader, which is entertainment.

options.text: A report on school attendance figures
options.feedback: A report of figures is informative and would not aim to amuse.

questions.explanation: A text written to entertain aims to give the reader pleasure, usually through a story or a humorous situation.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the text and identify its purpose: 'Because the road will be closed on Friday, the school bus will pick you up two streets earlier than usual.'
questions.context: A reading comprehension exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To argue against closing roads in the city
options.feedback: The text accepts the closure and works with it rather than objecting to it.

options.text: To inform readers about a change to the bus route
options.feedback: The sentence gives practical information about an alteration caused by roadworks.

options.text: To describe the history of the bus route
options.feedback: No historical background appears in the notice.

options.text: To entertain readers with an amusing anecdote
options.feedback: The tone is practical and factual, with no aim to amuse.

questions.explanation: The text explains a change caused by roadworks so that passengers can adapt, which is a practical informative purpose.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the difference between a text written to inform and one written to persuade?
questions.context: A reading strategy lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: An informative text presents facts; a persuasive one argues for a position.
options.feedback: The first aims at understanding and the second at convincing, which is the core difference.

options.text: They are exactly the same, because both report facts.
options.feedback: A persuasive text uses facts to support an argument, which is a different aim.

options.text: An informative text is always shorter than a persuasive one.
options.feedback: Length is a matter of subject matter, not of purpose.

options.text: A persuasive text never mentions facts at all.
options.feedback: Persuasive writing often relies heavily on facts and figures as evidence.

questions.explanation: An informative text presents facts, while a persuasive text argues for a position and tries to change the reader's mind.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that signals an argumentative text.
questions.context: A reading comprehension exercise in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The school day begins at seven o'clock and ends at one in the afternoon.
options.feedback: This is a plain statement of fact with no position being argued for.

options.text: In my view, the school day should start later, because students sleep badly otherwise.
options.feedback: The phrase 'in my view' and the word 'because' present a claim with its reason, which is argument.

options.text: The bell rings at seven o'clock every weekday morning.
options.feedback: Reporting a fixed routine is informative, not argumentative.

options.text: The playground is on the other side of the building.
options.feedback: Giving a location is informative and takes no position at all.

questions.explanation: An argumentative text asks the reader to accept a claim, so it uses words such as 'therefore', 'in my view' or 'clearly' to push a position.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a text that gives directions for reaching a place?
questions.context: A reading comprehension task in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To describe the history of the place
options.feedback: Nothing in a set of directions concerns origins or dates.

options.text: To persuade the reader to visit the place
options.feedback: Directions help a reader find a place; they do not argue for visiting it.

options.text: To entertain the reader with local customs
options.feedback: A description of customs would be a different text with a different purpose.

options.text: To instruct the reader on how to get somewhere
options.feedback: Directions exist to lead a reader from one place to another.

questions.explanation: Giving directions so that a reader can find a place is an instructional purpose, since the aim is that the reader can act on the information.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a text that opens with 'Dear Customer' and closes with 'Yours faithfully'?
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To tell a fictional story
options.feedback: A story does not use a salutation or a formal sign-off.

options.text: To describe a scientific process
options.feedback: A scientific text uses impersonal verbs rather than a letter format.

options.text: To write a formal letter
options.feedback: The salutation and the closing are the conventions of a formal letter.

options.text: To list prices for customers
options.feedback: A price list is informative and would not include a sign-off.

questions.explanation: The formal opening and closing mark a letter, so the text exists to communicate with a particular reader in an official way.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read and identify the purpose: 'The following three sections explain how to apply, how to renew and how to cancel a membership.'
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To explain how to carry out three procedures
options.feedback: Each section gives instructions the reader can follow, which is instructional.

options.text: To argue that memberships are unnecessary
options.feedback: No argument against memberships appears in the text.

options.text: To describe the history of the organisation
options.feedback: The sentence concerns current procedures, not past history.

options.text: To persuade readers to become members
options.feedback: The text explains how to use a membership but does not promote joining one.

questions.explanation: The text lays out procedures step by step so that a reader can carry them out, which is an instructional purpose.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A text describes the causes of a landslide that blocked a road. What is its purpose?
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To entertain readers with a dramatic story
options.feedback: The aim is factual explanation, not amusement.

options.text: To persuade readers to avoid the road entirely
options.feedback: The text explains the cause but makes no recommendation of that kind.

options.text: To give instructions for clearing the road
options.feedback: The text describes causes rather than instructing anyone to act.

options.text: To explain why the event happened
options.feedback: The text investigates causes, which makes it explanatory and therefore informative.

questions.explanation: Explaining why something happened is an informative purpose, since the reader's understanding is the aim.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which text has a persuasive purpose?
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: This route runs for eleven kilometres and passes through three towns.
options.feedback: It reports measurable facts without arguing for a choice.

options.text: We strongly recommend this route, because it avoids the steep climb and saves nearly an hour.
options.feedback: It recommends a course of action and supplies the reasons for doing so.

options.text: The route was closed for repairs during the month of March.
options.feedback: That is a neutral statement of fact about an event.

options.text: Mountain roads in the region are built with wide hairpin bends.
options.feedback: The sentence generalises about construction without recommending anything.

questions.explanation: A persuasive text takes a position and gives reasons so that the reader is convinced.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read and identify the purpose: 'Turn left after the bridge, walk for two hundred metres and then turn right at the school gate.'
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To direct a reader to a location
options.feedback: The imperative verbs describe the route step by step.

options.text: To persuade the reader to visit the school
options.feedback: The sentence gives directions and makes no invitation at all.

options.text: To describe the history of the bridge
options.feedback: No historical information appears in the directions given.

options.text: To explain why the road was closed
options.feedback: The sentence concerns directions, not reasons for any closure.

questions.explanation: A sequence of instructions the reader can follow is an instructional text intended to guide someone to a place.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a text that reports what happened at a town meeting?
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To argue that the decisions taken were wrong
options.feedback: That would require reasons and a position, which reporting does not supply.

options.text: To persuade people to attend the next meeting
options.feedback: A report describes the past meeting rather than advertising another one.

options.text: To report the events of the meeting
options.feedback: The text recounts what occurred so that readers can know about it.

options.text: To instruct readers on how to hold a meeting
options.feedback: The text is not a guide to procedure; it reports one specific case.

questions.explanation: Reporting an event accurately for those who could not attend is an informative purpose.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How can a reader tell a text is written to persuade?
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: It contains a list of dates and figures only
options.feedback: Facts appear in informative writing and can also support an argument.

options.text: It contains a position supported by reasons
options.feedback: A claim with evidence aimed at agreement is the marker of persuasive writing.

options.text: It is always printed in a newspaper
options.feedback: Medium does not determine the purpose of a text.

options.text: It contains no paragraphs at all
options.feedback: Persuasive texts are usually well organised into paragraphs.

questions.explanation: Persuasive writing contains a claim and supporting reasons, usually marked by words such as 'therefore' or 'clearly'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read and identify the purpose: 'Twenty years ago the factory employed three hundred people; today it employs twelve.'
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To present a contrastive comparison of employment
options.feedback: The two figures are compared to show how the situation changed.

options.text: To argue that the factory should close
options.feedback: The text reports figures without recommending any action.

options.text: To entertain readers with a story about workers
options.feedback: There is no narrative element in a bare statistical comparison.

options.text: To explain how to apply for a job there
options.feedback: The sentence says nothing about how to find work in the factory.

questions.explanation: The sentence sets two figures against each other so the reader can see the decline, which is an informative contrast.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the text that is mainly informative rather than persuasive.
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: You simply must visit this museum, because it is the finest in the region.
options.feedback: The imperative and the superlative push the reader towards a decision.

options.text: Everyone agrees that this museum deserves more funding than it receives.
options.feedback: The appeal for funding states a position the reader is expected to share.

options.text: The museum contains more than four hundred paintings from the sixteenth century onwards.
options.feedback: The sentence presents a verifiable fact and argues for nothing.

options.text: In my opinion the museum is far too small for its collection.
options.feedback: The phrase 'in my opinion' announces a personal judgement to be accepted.

questions.explanation: An informative text presents facts without taking a position, while a persuasive one argues for one.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read and identify the purpose: 'If you are allergic to any ingredient, tell the kitchen before you order.'
questions.context: A reading skills lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To describe the ingredients in the kitchen
options.feedback: The sentence says nothing about the ingredients themselves.

options.text: To warn that the restaurant may close soon
options.feedback: No mention of closing appears in the sentence.

options.text: To persuade customers to choose a different restaurant
options.feedback: The sentence keeps the reader inside this restaurant and gives advice.

options.text: To instruct a reader on what to do before ordering
options.feedback: It gives a conditional instruction the reader can act on directly.

questions.explanation: The sentence gives a practical instruction for a safe course of action, which is an instructional purpose.
questions.subject: ingles
